titre: Only One County Was Big Enough to Apply It
accroche: In 1899, Illinois creates a court for children, reserved for counties of more than 500,000 inhabitants: in 1900, only one county reaches that threshold.
contenu_vulgarise:
Before the juvenile court, children as young as seven are sent to the same jails as adult criminals. According to Wikipedia, in 1898, 508 offenses are committed by children aged ten or younger, and 15,161 by children and teenagers between ten and twenty. Illinois has no mechanism of its own for dealing with these children: they are charged, jailed, and punished like adults.

Lucy Flower, a Chicago philanthropist, carries the project: she wins the support of Illinois social-work leaders and assists a Chicago Bar Association committee tasked with drafting the text. Julia Lathrop and Jane Addams are among those who help create the court; Lathrop will later head the women's committee that raises funds to pay probation officers. The project does not aim to punish children less severely, but to treat them differently: as children who need help, not as scaled-down criminals.

## One Law, One County

The law applies to counties of more than five hundred thousand inhabitants. In Illinois, according to the 1900 census table reproduced in the New International Encyclopædia, only Cook County, home to Chicago, exceeds that threshold, with 1,838,735 inhabitants. The court opens in early July 1899: on July 3, Judge Richard S. Tuthill holds the first hearing, in which a mother accuses her eleven-year-old son of theft; rather than sending him to a penal institution, the judge places him with his grandmother. The procedure is looser than in adult courts: no mandatory lawyer, social workers, probation officers, separation from adult inmates. It rests on *parens patriae*, an old equity jurisdiction under which the state may protect a child in place of failing parents, without this amounting to a punishment.

## What Chicago Exports

Colorado adopts a comparable law in 1903; by 1925, a juvenile court exists, in one form or another, in every American state but two. Encyclopedia.com presents the Cook County court as the first of its kind in the world. The idea that a delinquent child is first a matter of protection, and only then of punishment, starts from a county whose population exceeded a threshold that Illinois's other counties did not reach.

repere.texte: Before the Cook County juvenile court, opened on July 1, 1899 according to Wikipedia, children as young as seven were sent to the same jails as adult criminals. In 1898, 508 offenses are committed by children aged ten or younger.

carte.punch: A population threshold decided which American children would escape adult prison.
carte.idee: In 1899, Illinois law creates a juvenile court, but only in counties of more than five hundred thousand inhabitants. In 1900, only one Illinois county reaches that threshold: Cook, home to Chicago.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full story of one of the three women behind the world's first juvenile court.

quiz.question: Why does the 1899 law create a juvenile court only in Cook County?
choix: Because the rest of Illinois already had juvenile courts
Because the law reserved this court for children under ten
Because a ruling of the federal Supreme Court had required it for Chicago
Because the law sets a population threshold that only this county reached in 1900
quiz.explication: The law targets counties of more than five hundred thousand inhabitants; in 1900, only Cook County, home to Chicago, exceeds that threshold. No other juvenile court existed before it, the law does not target only children under ten, and no federal ruling required it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which legal principle, drawn from an old equity jurisdiction, justifies the state stepping in for failing parents?
choix: The principle that punishments must be set by law
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1899 law is described by Illinois courts as a codification of the old equity jurisdiction over children, parens patriae: the state protects the child in place of failing parents, without this amounting to a punishment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Judge Richard S. Tuthill decide at the court's first hearing, on July 3, 1899?
choix: He acquits the accused child for lack of evidence
He places the child with his grandmother rather than in a reformatory
He sends the case to an adult court
He orders the immediate closure of the new court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rather than a placement in a reformatory, Tuthill places the eleven-year-old accused of theft with his grandmother, at the court's very first hearing, on July 3, 1899.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who drafts the 1899 bill with Lucy Flower's help?
choix: A committee of the federal Supreme Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Encyclopedia.com, Lucy Flower assists a Chicago Bar Association committee that drafts the text of the law.
